headline: Lixi Ye and Baitian Li post a Subset Sum algorithm running in O(2^0.4999977n), the first worst-case improvement on the meet-in-the-middle bound that has stood since 1974, and cite a machine-written preprint from three days earlier claiming far more.

items.title: Print the bottom transistor from the back of the wafer
items.dek: Geert Hellings of imec describes a new complementary-FET flow — the scheme that stacks a p-type transistor directly above an n-type one — that starts from two bonded wafers, prints the upper device from the front, then flips and thins the wafer and prints the lower device from the back.
items.why_it_matters: Building both devices from one front-side stack forces two sets of source–drain contacts, the dielectric that keeps the two gates at different threshold voltages, and the local wiring into a single trench between gates roughly twice as tall as a nanosheet cell's, and that aspect ratio is what has held monolithic stacking back. Patterning the lower device from the opposite face trades the trench for a registration problem, and imec's own backside EUV work quotes overlay better than 3 nm, so the binding constraint moves from how deep you can etch to how well you can align one side of a wafer to the other.
items.background_md: A standard cell's width is set largely by the side-by-side spacing an n-type and a p-type transistor need, and that spacing has stopped shrinking as fast as the gate pitch has. Stacking the two vertically removes it from the cell width, which is where the next step in logic density is supposed to come from: cell height is counted in routing tracks, and a three-track cell is not reachable with the two devices sitting beside each other. The price is that everything once reached from above — contacts, gate isolation, local wiring — now has to serve two device tiers at once.
items.deeper_md:
The flow imec calls double-flip sequential CFET starts from a bonded stack with a middle dielectric isolation layer already embedded in it. The top device is patterned from the front, the wafer is flipped and thinned, the bottom device is patterned from the back, an optional via joins the two gates where a common gate is wanted, and a second flip finishes the wafer. Common-gate devices cover roughly 90–95 percent of basic logic gates; flip-flops and multiplexers are what need the two gates driven independently, which is what the split-gate variant and its extra via buy.

The cell-level claims are about 98 percent layout efficiency, the best of the architectures compared, and three-track cells reaching A3 and A2 — against 5.5-track nanosheet cells down to A10 and 4.5-track CFET cells from A7. The SRAM number is the concrete one. A conventional 6T bit cell maps badly onto stacked devices because both its pass gates are n-type, leaving the two p-type devices above them idle; replacing the pair with one split-gate CFET transmission gate gives a 5T+1 cell about 12.5 percent smaller than the 6T CFET version that writes 7–15 percent faster.

All of it is design-technology co-optimisation on a virtual flow, published by the institute whose roadmap it supports, and the three 2026 VLSI papers behind the numbers are cited without links. imec also wants the contacted-poly-pitch to metal-1 gear ratio raised from about 1:1 to 2:1 at A7, which is an admission that frontside routing rather than the device is now the congested part.

glossary.definition: A cell built with the p-type transistor stacked directly above the n-type one instead of beside it, so the n-to-p spacing leaves the cell width and becomes a vertical process problem.
Cell height measured in routing-metal pitches, so a three-track cell is three metal pitches tall; it fixes density more directly than the node name does.
The insulator placed between the stacked upper and lower gates, which is what lets the two devices carry different threshold voltages instead of sharing one gate stack.
The ratio of contacted poly pitch to metal-1 pitch; raising it gives a cell more wiring tracks per gate, and costs a finer metal-1 pitch that has to be printed.

items.fab_angle: Front-to-back registration is a different measurement from layer-to-layer overlay: the marks sit on the face you are not printing on, so you either read them through the silicon in the infrared or etch a second set into the backside before bonding — a decision a maskless stepper has to make before its first double-sided layer, not after.

items.title: The p-type gallium oxide is a second phase handing over electrons
items.dek: Dong Su Yu, Hongping Zhao and co-authors report that their LiGa₅O₈ films — a spinel oxide with a bandgap near 5.4 electronvolts — conduct holes only when a second crystal phase of β-gallium oxide is present, and credit the holes to charge transfer across that internal interface rather than to any dopant.
items.why_it_matters: Every attempt at p-type conduction in this oxide family hits the same wall: the acceptor states on offer sit a few tenths of an electronvolt to more than one electronvolt above the valence band, deep enough to keep their holes, and the same group's 2024 calculation said lithium vacancies here are no exception. If the carriers instead come from one phase donating electrons into the other's deep acceptors, then the quantities to control are phase fraction and band offset, and a clean single-phase film is the wrong thing to aim for.
items.background_md: An ultra-wide-bandgap oxide is straightforward to dope n-type and close to impossible to dope p-type, and the reason is band structure rather than chemistry. The valence band is built from oxygen 2p states that barely disperse, so a hole is heavy, and it becomes energetically favourable for it to sit on a single oxygen atom with the lattice relaxed around it — a self-trapped hole, which carries no current. Native oxygen vacancies then donate electrons that cancel whatever acceptors were added, pinning the Fermi level away from the valence band.
items.deeper_md:
The films are grown by mist chemical vapour deposition, and the experiment is a comparison rather than a single sample: some growth conditions give hole conduction and others give insulating films. The conductive ones carry room-temperature hole concentrations on the order of 10¹⁸ cm⁻³. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy finds a lower Li/Ga ratio in those films, so they are lithium-deficient, and Raman spectroscopy together with X-ray diffraction finds β-Ga₂O₃ signatures in them that the insulating films do not have. The proposed mechanism joins a previously reported type-II alignment between the two phases to the calculated lithium-vacancy acceptor levels: electrons leave the β-Ga₂O₃ valence band for the deeper LiGa₅O₈ acceptor states, and the holes left behind are the carriers.

That is charge-transfer doping rather than substitutional doping, and it is the opening the earlier calculation left. Dabsamut, Takahashi and Lambrecht put the LiGa₅O₈ gap at about 5.36 eV, found lithium vacancies somewhat shallower than the same defect in LiGaO₂ but still not shallow enough to ionise, and concluded that donors dominate, so an equilibrium Fermi level would be pinned deep in the gap.

The caveats are the ones a two-phase film always carries. A single Hall number measured on a mixture cannot be assigned to one phase, no mobility accompanies the carrier concentration, and the charge transfer is inferred from the correlation between phase content and conduction rather than measured directly. Lambrecht co-authored both the 2024 calculation and this preprint, so theory and experiment are not independent here.

glossary.definition: A hole that lowers its own energy by localising on one atom and letting the surrounding lattice distort around it; once trapped it stops conducting, which is why a flat valence band blocks p-type conduction.
A junction where both the conduction and valence band edges of one material sit below the other's, so electrons and holes are driven to opposite sides instead of staying together.

A missing lithium atom in the lattice; it leaves the surrounding oxygen short of an electron, which makes it an acceptor, and how far above the valence band that acceptor level sits decides whether it ever gives up a hole.

Supplying carriers from an adjacent material across a band offset rather than from an impurity inside the crystal, so the carrier count is set by interface area and offset instead of by dopant concentration.

items.title: Meta gives each host its own packet buffer, and loses the shared pool
items.dek: Meta has published the ten-month operating record of fbnic, the network interface chip it designed to serve several server blades from one card, and the architectural choice it credits is partitioning: each host gets its own MAC, firmware instance, PCIe interface and packet buffers rather than a shared pool.
items.why_it_matters: The vendor parts fbnic replaced ran every host on a sled through one packet buffer as small as 512 kilobytes, so a slow receiver or a microburst on one host dropped packets for its neighbours, and a firmware fault on one host could take the sled and its management controller off the network entirely. Partitioning ends that failure class by giving up statistical multiplexing: each host now has a dedicated 384 kilobyte receive buffer where the vendor card offered roughly 700 kilobytes of shared pool, so a host that stalls its own PCIe bus has less headroom, not more.
items.background_md: A multi-host network interface card gives several independent servers in one chassis a single shared card and a single network link, which saves ports, optics, cabling and power. The tension is that the servers are meant to be separate failure domains and the card is one piece of hardware: the receive queues, the packet buffer, the management path and the link itself are shared among tenants that know nothing about each other. Whether each host is handed a fixed slice of those resources or draws from a common pool is the decision the rest of the design follows from.
items.deeper_md:
The card runs on hundreds of thousands of production hosts, up from a few thousand inside a year, with the fleet growing about 130× over the measurement window. Against a vendor multi-host NIC on the same platform, unplanned unavailability fell from 9.11 percent to 0.74 percent, the hardware swap rate from 6.7 to 2.9 percent, and mean time to repair from 197.9 to 125.5 hours.

The case for partitioning is the failure the paper leads with: a vendor firmware bug made the NIC emit Ethernet pause frames indefinitely after a PCIe error on one host, which rendered every host on the sled and its management controller unreachable. It touched more than 1,500 racks and potentially over 14,000 hosts, and the vendor took 52 weeks to ship a fix. The second lever is interface size — fbnic defines fewer than ten runtime firmware message types, three of them request/response pairs, against more than 170 Ethernet firmware opcodes on a representative vendor part, which is what makes the driver rather than the firmware the layer you can fix yourself.

The measurement is Meta's, of Meta's hardware, against a vendor it does not name. Months eight and nine regressed as the fleet roughly tripled and a rack-switch interoperability problem appeared, and a PXE boot bug plus a switch PHY interaction accounted for about 60 percent of fbnic repairs in the window. Table 1 lists two hosts per NIC on the 2024 platform at 100G each while the die carries four slices, and the paper does not reconcile the two.

glossary.definition: One network card wired to several independent servers in a chassis, each with its own PCIe link to the card, so one chip and one network port serve machines that are otherwise unrelated.
An Ethernet flow-control message asking the link partner to stop sending for a time; a device that emits them continuously silences its own link, which is why one host's bug could mute a whole card.
The small always-on processor that powers, monitors and recovers a server out of band; if it loses its network path the machine can only be fixed by hand at the rack.
Average elapsed time from a fault being detected to the machine being back in service, which in a datacentre is dominated by queueing for a technician rather than by the repair itself.

items.title: Subset Sum finally drops below 2^(n/2)
items.dek: Lixi Ye and Baitian Li have posted a randomised algorithm that decides Subset Sum — given n integers, does some subset of them total exactly a target — in O(2^0.4999977n) time, the first worst-case improvement on the O(2^(n/2)) meet-in-the-middle bound published in 1974.
items.why_it_matters: The gain is one part in 450,000 of the exponent and its size is not the point, because the proof names what was in the way. The fastest known test of which half-solutions combine came from a Boolean circuit for the matching matrix, and Boolean circuits cannot push the relevant exponent below 1/4; allowing integer arithmetic, where terms can cancel, gets under 1/4, and the paper shows that anything under 1/4 converts mechanically into a sub-2^(n/2) algorithm. A fifty-two-year wall becomes a numerical optimisation.
items.background_md: Subset Sum is the standard setting in which exact exponential algorithms get measured, because the algorithm to beat is known and simple. Horowitz and Sahni showed in 1974 that you can split n items into halves, enumerate all 2^(n/2) subset sums of each half, sort one list and search the other, so brute force's 2^n becomes 2^(n/2) — and that stayed the best worst-case bound. Average-case versions have been beaten since, and the space has been cut below 2^(n/4) at the same running time, but the worst-case time exponent of 1/2 did not move.
items.deeper_md:
Theorem 4.1 gives a randomised algorithm with worst-case running time O(2^((1/2 − 1/450000)n)) in bit operations, assuming the input's total binary length is 2^o(n). It returns a correct subset with probability at least 99 percent when one exists, and never returns a wrong answer.

Three pieces do the work. Each candidate solution is written as a sum of two vectors using the redundant encodings 0 = 0+0 = 1+(−1) and 1 = 0+1 = 1+0 — the representation technique. Relabelling −1 as 1, 1 as 0 and 0 as a wildcard turns the compatibility test into partial match: does a binary string agree with a query everywhere the query specifies? Partial match is solved by factoring its matrix into two sparse matrices, a depth-2 linear circuit, costing each factor's degree times the list it multiplies. Boolean factorisations stop at exponent 1/4 — the Fredman–Volper construction — while an exact-integer factorisation using inclusion–exclusion with cancellation, a random covering of the wildcard sets and colour-indexed lookup tables gets below it, by a margin above 0.00002.

The authors call the mathematics complete and the presentation preliminary, the constant comes from truncated numerical optimisation certified by rational interval arithmetic, and no space bound is claimed. Their declaration discloses substantial AI assistance and cites a preprint dated 4 October 2026, attributed to an OpenAI model, claiming O(2^0.49n) on the same problem; that PDF did not render here, so it stands as a citation, not a checked result.

glossary.definition: Split the input in half, enumerate every partial answer on each side, and look for a matching pair; it trades exponential memory for a square-rooted running time.

Deliberately allowing each solution to be written in many different ways, which multiplies the number of partial answers but lets you keep only those passing a cheap filter, so fewer candidates survive to be matched.

Given strings and queries in which some positions are wildcards, decide whether a string agrees with a query everywhere the query is specified; the hard instance here has about half the positions wild.
A factorisation of a matrix into two sparse matrices, so applying it costs the nonzeros per row of one plus per column of the other; those two degrees are what the running time is paid in.

items.title: Break the arithmetic and bigger transformers mind it less
items.dek: Trevor McCourt, Ila Fiete and Isaac Chuang trained sixteen Llama2-style transformers while randomly zeroing four-element blocks inside every attention and feed-forward matrix multiply, and found the loss penalty from those faults shrinking as the models grew rather than compounding, which is the opposite of how an ordinary computation behaves.
items.why_it_matters: Dropping a chip's supply voltage saves energy roughly as the square of the voltage and raises the arithmetic error rate, so the standing obstacle is that a correction scheme's overhead grows with the size of the computation until it swallows the saving. The fitted curves here bend the other way: the share of parameters spent absorbing errors falls again above a critical model size, which is what a good error-correcting code does and plain redundancy cannot. If it holds, the hardware to build is a detector that turns a wrong product into a missing one and leaves the correcting to the network.
items.background_md: Arithmetic hardware is built to be exactly right, and a large share of its energy goes on guaranteeing that: supply voltage held well above the point where a transistor's switching becomes probabilistic, timing margin for the slowest path, and check bits on the memory. Cutting those margins saves energy and raises the error rate, so how wrong a computation may be is an energy question rather than a purely logical one. Classical fault tolerance answers it with redundancy — repeat the work, or add parity — and pays a fixed multiple on every operation, which is the overhead a very large computation cannot absorb.
items.deeper_md:
The fault model is narrow and stated. Only the operands of the matrix products in attention — the Q, K, V and output projections and the QKᵀ and AV products — and in the feed-forward block are corrupted; embeddings, readout, normalisation, nonlinearities and residual additions stay exact. Operands are masked along the contraction axis in contiguous four-element blocks, each zeroed independently with probability p, with a fresh mask per sequence every forward pass. That assumes an arbitrary-magnitude error has already been detected and converted into a zero, which is the job of the accelerator they sketch, checking a residue every few fused multiply–adds.

Seventeen values of p from 0 to 0.2, sixteen decoder-only models from 7.9 × 10⁶ to 9.3 × 10⁸ parameters trained on 7.9 × 10⁷ to 3.5 × 10¹⁰ tokens, two seeds per cell, about 40,000 GPU-hours. Loss is fitted as a floor plus exp(α₀ − α₁n − α₂n²) plus exp(β₀ − β₁d) in log model size n and log data d. The new term is the quadratic α₂, pinned to zero at p = 0, and it is what makes the fraction of parameters doing useful work a parabola in log size: falling, then rising past a critical size.

No real faulty silicon was used, nothing above about 10⁹ parameters was trained, the error floor was fixed near 1.5 rather than fitted, and the threshold claim is explicitly a conjecture; the authors put the compute to test 10¹¹ parameters at roughly 10²⁶ FLOPs.

glossary.definition: The dimension a matrix product sums over, so zeroing a block of it deletes a contiguous run of the terms inside every dot product rather than corrupting one output.
A fitted formula predicting a model's loss from its parameter count and its training-token count, used to extrapolate what a larger run would achieve before paying for it.
The fraction of an error-correcting code's symbols that carry payload rather than redundancy; a code is called good when that fraction stays bounded away from zero as the block gets longer.
The multiply-then-accumulate primitive that matrix hardware is built out of and billed in; the proposed checker verifies a residue after every few of them.

items.title: One sign error withdraws three machine-written papers
items.dek: OpenAI's public repository of mathematics produced by an unreleased model logged its first dated corrections on 7 October, withdrawing three manuscripts after a sign error in one of them broke both its own argument and a construction the other two had imported, and leaving 300 of 719 headline results machine-checked in Lean.
items.why_it_matters: The unit that failed is the dependency rather than the paper: one bad construction took down three manuscripts, which is the failure mode a corpus generated in bulk is most exposed to and the one a per-paper error rate cannot see. It also sorts the collection in two, because the 300 results a proof checker has accepted are wrong only if Lean's kernel is wrong, while the other 419 are correct only in the sense that nobody reading them has objected yet — and the repository says as much about them itself.
items.background_md: A proof assistant checks a proof by requiring every inference to be a term its small trusted kernel can typecheck, which turns "is this proof correct" into a decidable question about a file. What it does not check is that the statement formalised is the statement intended, or that an informal paper's lemmas match the formal ones; those remain acts of human reading. A collection of mathematics therefore splits into a part a machine has verified and a part whose correctness is still a claim about attention, and the two halves fail in different ways.
items.deeper_md:
The repository holds 719 manuscripts in 372 result families. Its README says the vast majority came from one procedure with an unreleased model, averaging about three hours of thinking per result across roughly 4,000 posed problems, with outputs grouped into families and filtered by a significance threshold it does not describe; two results are named as exceptions, a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties.

The 7 October entry is the first dated release in the history file. Three manuscripts are withdrawn — on algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds, on Kuga–Satake correspondences for K3 surfaces, and on the rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces — each now carrying a notice and a link to the archived text, because a sign error in the first invalidated a stabilisation-trace cancellation argument and a construction the other two used. Fourteen further manuscripts were revised across five clusters, thirteen companion manuscripts were updated to cite the revised editions, and six new formalisations brought machine-checked headline results to 300 of 719, about 42 percent.

All of that is the publisher's account of its own corpus, with no independent audit, and the README's own warning is that unformalised results could have issues. Two numbers are worth holding apart: the 42 percent counts headline results and not the lemmas beneath them, and the roughly 4,000 posed problems is a denominator for the filter rather than for the mathematics.

glossary.definition: Software that accepts a proof only when every step typechecks against a small trusted kernel, so trusting the proof reduces to trusting a few thousand lines of checker rather than a reader's attention.

The headline theorem a manuscript claims, as opposed to the lemmas supporting it; the formalisation fraction quoted here is counted over these, so an unformalised lemma can sit under a formalised headline.
A group of manuscripts in this repository that share a problem and build on one another, which makes the family rather than the file the unit an error propagates through.

The unstated filter the publisher applied to decide which model outputs became manuscripts, which is why the count of posed problems and the count of published manuscripts cannot be divided into a success rate.

foundations.subtitle: Why a ring, two spots or four of them beats a filled circle of light, and what the shape costs in compute.
foundations.tldr: The light that falls on a photomask is a designed object, not a lamp pointed at glass. Its shape inside the illuminator's pupil decides which diffraction orders from the mask get collected by the projection lens, and therefore which pitches print at all. Shaping it buys resolution for free; the bill arrives as an optimum that is specific to one pattern and that nobody can work out by hand.

sections.heading: The pupil is where the image is decided
sections.body_md:
Start with the thing a lithography tool does with its light. Köhler illumination images the source into the pupil rather than onto the mask, so each point of the source becomes one *direction* of plane-wave illumination arriving at the mask, and the brightness across the field is uniform even if the lamp is not. A mask with pitch p diffracts each incoming plane wave into orders at angles where sin θ = m·λ/p, measured from that wave's own direction. The projection lens collects only rays inside its numerical aperture, so the pupil behaves as a hard aperture in angle: an order that falls outside NA is not attenuated, it is absent.

Now send the light in straight on. The zeroth order sits at the centre of the pupil and the two first orders at ±λ/p. If λ/p exceeds NA both first orders miss the lens entirely, only the uniform zeroth order survives, and the aerial image has no modulation whatsoever. No dose and no resist chemistry recovers a pattern that is not there.
sections.deeper_md: This is the origin of the familiar two-beam limit. Keep the zeroth order and one first order inside the pupil and the printable half-pitch is λ/(4·NA), which is k₁ = 0.25. Below that the orders have left the pupil and no amount of process is relevant. Everything called resolution enhancement is an attempt to approach 0.25 from above; everything called multipatterning is an admission that you cannot go under it.

sections.heading: Tilt the light and the orders come back inside
sections.body_md:
Off-axis illumination is the fix, and it is one line of geometry. Move the source point out to a normalised pupil radius σ, and the whole diffraction fan moves with it: the zeroth order shifts off-centre by σ·NA, and one of the first orders shifts inward by the same amount. Choose σ so that the zeroth order sits near one edge of the pupil and one first order near the opposite edge, and you have two beams inside the lens interfering at the full pitch frequency — at a pitch the on-axis system could not resolve at all.

The cost is paid immediately. The other first order has left the pupil, so the image is formed by two beams rather than three, which changes the contrast and the way it behaves through focus. σ itself is the illumination numerical aperture divided by the projection numerical aperture, so it is a number between zero and one, and annular settings are quoted as an inner and an outer σ: a 2024 source-mask optimisation paper initialises its source at σ_i = 0.63 and σ_o = 0.95. Large σ approaches incoherent illumination, small σ approaches coherent.

sections.heading: Which shape, and why the answer is per-layer
sections.body_md:
Given that geometry, the shapes are not arbitrary. A dipole puts two poles exactly where the required orders have to come from, which maximises contrast for one-dimensional dense lines in a single orientation and prints nothing useful for lines rotated by ninety degrees. A quadrupole, or quasar, uses four poles to serve two orthogonal orientations at once, which is what a Manhattan layout needs. An annulus is the compromise you reach for when a layer contains many pitches and many orientations, because a ring has some energy at every azimuth and no azimuth gets the best of it.

The consequence is the part worth remembering. Since the pitch is what sets the σ at which the orders land correctly, a source tuned for one pitch mis-serves another, and the pitches in between can be worse than either endpoint. That is why illumination is chosen per layer rather than per tool, why layouts get decomposed by orientation before they are exposed, and why "what illumination are you running" is a question about a mask layer.

sections.heading: A worked optimisation, and its four numbers
sections.body_md:
Here is what that looks like when someone actually does it. Pomplun and co-authors optimise a quadrupole described by exactly four parameters — two segment opening angles b₁ and b₂, and two inner radii r₁ and r₂ — for a hole-cutting layer at λ = 193 nm, NA 1.35, 4× reduction, on a mask pitch of 704 nm in both directions with an absorber of n = 0.84 and k = 1.65.

Scanning the mask geometry alone, the best hole came out at width 160 nm, height 488 nm, depth 40 nm. Optimising source and mask together landed on r₁ = 0.74, r₂ = 0.89, b₁ = 43.4°, b₂ = 44.9°, with the mask at 160.0, 499.7 and 39.1 nm. Notice which half moved: the mask barely changed and the illumination did the work.

The compute is the other half of the story. One rigorous finite-element solve of that mask has 341,440 unknowns and takes about 10,000 seconds of CPU time for the eighteen plane waves needed (nine incoming directions, two polarisations each). A reduced-basis surrogate built from forty snapshot solutions answers in about one second — four orders of magnitude — which is what turns a thousand forward evaluations from an estimated month into roughly an hour on a desktop.

sections.heading: From a hole plate to four thousand mirrors
sections.body_md:
For most of the history of this idea the pupil shape was a diffractive optical element physically inserted into the illuminator and swapped by hand whenever the setting changed. ASML's description of its DUV free-form illuminator, FlexRay, is an array of 4,000 individually controllable mirrors that can form essentially any pupil shape instantly; FlexPupil does the same job on its EUV tools.

Once the source is a programmable map rather than a chosen stencil, the optimisation changes character: the source stops being four parameters and becomes a grid of pixels, co-optimised with the mask. In a 2024 bilevel method the source is a 35 × 35 greyscale map squashed through a sigmoid and the mask is a 2048 × 2048 image, with the aerial image computed in Abbe form — a sum of coherent images, one per effective source point — again at 193 nm and NA 1.35. Treating the source as an inner problem solved inside the mask optimisation cut turnaround from 122.5–287 seconds per tile to 12.6–15.3 seconds, with roughly forty percent lower edge-placement error and process-variation band than alternating the two.

sections.heading: EUV changes which problem the shape is solving
sections.body_md:
At 13.5 nm nothing transmits, so every surface is a reflector and the mask is necessarily illuminated at an angle. That makes illumination design part of the projector's geometry rather than a setting layered on top of it, and the trade-offs move accordingly.

A concrete illustration is Shintake's proposal for a simplified two-mirror in-line EUV projector, where the pupil carries a central obscuration and symmetric quadrupole off-axis illumination is used specifically to place the useful orders around that obscuration while still realising Köhler illumination. His estimates for the design are 0.2 NA over a 20 mm field with a 24 nm theoretical resolution limit, or 0.3 NA over a 10 mm field reaching 16 nm with a curved mask, at 20 W of EUV source power for 100 wafers an hour — about a tenth of what he attributes to a conventional six-mirror system — with a 2000 mm object-to-image distance.

Two cautions. It is a design proposal and not a built tool. And the power saving there is credited to mirror count, not to the pupil shape, so it is not evidence about what shaping a pupil costs in photons.

glossary.definition: An arrangement that images the source into the pupil instead of onto the mask, so every source point becomes an illumination direction and the field brightness is uniform regardless of how uneven the source is.

The plane in which the optical system's angular acceptance is a physical aperture; a position in the pupil corresponds to a direction at the mask, which is why drawing shapes there is the same as choosing angles.

Illumination numerical aperture divided by projection numerical aperture, a number between 0 and 1 giving the radius in the pupil at which light enters; an annulus is quoted as an inner and an outer σ.
One of the discrete directions a periodic mask sends light into, at sin θ = m·λ/p for pitch p; the image exists only if at least two orders are collected by the lens.
How far a printed feature edge sits from where the design put it, in nanometres; it is the metric optimisers minimise because it is what actually breaks a circuit.
The area swept out by a printed edge as dose and focus move across their tolerance, so a smaller band means the pattern survives a wider process window rather than merely printing once.

foundations.try_this: Put a number on your own illuminator. With the DMD driven all-on and no reticle in the path, measure the diameter of the illuminated patch at the projection lens entrance pupil and divide it by the pupil diameter — that is your σ. Then expose the same dense line–space target twice, once with the full condenser aperture and once through an annular stop cut from card that blocks the inner sixty percent, and compare the finest pitch that clears. Read the quadrupole parameterisation in Pomplun et al. and write down the equivalent four numbers for your own condenser, even if two of them are zero.
